claims.statement: Wrike entered public beta on December 13, 2006.
Wrike combines task and project tracking with request forms, proofing, custom workflows, automation, reports, resource planning, documents, and AI features.
Free costs $0, Team is listed at $10 per user per month, and Business is $25 per user per month. Displayed paid prices are billed yearly.
Flexible workflows, forms, reports, dashboards, and cross-team organization are the strongest repeated benefits.
Learning effort, administration, seat groups, annual billing, feature gates, and uneven support are the main repeated limits.

scoreRationale.onboarding: Basic task use is approachable, but a useful company-wide setup needs decisions about spaces, fields, forms, statuses, access, templates, and training.
scoreRationale.product: Wrike is strong when several teams need one configurable system for requests, work, review, and reporting. It is excessive for a small team that only needs a shared task list.
scoreRationale.support: Implementation help can matter because the product is broad. Public feedback about support and onboarding is mixed, and no request was tested.
scoreRationale.billing: Current entry prices are public, but annual billing, seat groups, feature gates, paid add-ons, and quoted upper plans make the real bill less simple.
scoreRationale.overall: Build one real request-to-completion process with ordinary users, a manager, and an outside reviewer. Buy only if it replaces other tracking and the exact seat quote remains worthwhile.

conflictsAndUnknowns: Wrike can feel intuitive for ordinary tasks and complex once a company adds its own fields, rules, reports, and access model.
Its broad feature set can replace scattered tools and create a large system that needs an owner.
Current product quality and frustration with current commercial terms can coexist.
No hands-on setup, proofing, reporting, mobile, billing, or support test was completed.
